simple: a written plan for a piece of software, made before the code, that says what will be built, how, and how we will know it works.
analogy: the house blueprint that every builder signs before the first brick.
precise: in this university, a dated, reviewed document that records the context, goals and non-goals, the design and its interfaces, the alternatives considered, the failure modes, the test plan and the open questions of a change; the driver-specific design note of DR401 (one row per aspect of curriculum table 5.4) is one section of it. The curriculum's runbook asks for "a short design note" before code D2; design documents as a team practice are discussed in D1 D1.
source: F12-01 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: a test, agreed in advance, that decides whether the work is done.
analogy: the inspector's checklist, written before building, that the house must pass.
precise: an executable check (a host test, an emulator scenario with expected serial output, a measurement against a target) that is written down in the plan before the implementation and is not weakened afterwards without the approver's agreement; the curriculum's milestones list theirs and its definition of done requires all of them to pass from a clean build D2.
source: F12-01 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: one specific way a thing can go wrong.
analogy: "what if it rains before the roof is on?"
precise: a named condition under which a component cannot do its normal job (input arrives too fast, a device stops answering, a counter reaches its largest value, a caller passes a value out of range) together with the component's chosen behaviour in that condition. Curriculum rule 10 lists failure modes as one of the four things a plan must cover D2.
source: F12-01 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: every decision in the plan has a test, and every test says which decision it checks.
analogy: the inspector's checklist refers to numbered lines on the blueprint.
precise: a two-way mapping between identifiers in the plan (here D1–D3, F1–F3) and acceptance tests (here P1–P5), kept in the test names and the plan, so that a test failure leads to a decision and a decision without a test is visible. This is the course's convention; the lab in this chapter uses it.
source: F12-01 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: something the design deliberately does not try to do.
analogy: "this house will not have a basement", written on the blueprint so nobody digs.
precise: an explicit statement in a design document that a plausible requirement is out of scope for this change, so that reviewers do not judge the design against it and implementers do not build it; a non-goal may become a goal of a later document. This is the course's definition; D1 discusses goals and non-goals of design documents D1.
source: F12-02 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: the exact promise a function or module makes to whoever calls it, and what it expects in return.
analogy: the legend of the blueprint: what every symbol and every number means.
precise: for each operation: parameters with types, units and allowed ranges (preconditions); results and side effects (postconditions); who owns memory before and after; from which context it may be called (task, interrupt, any CPU); how errors and timeouts are reported. The course's checklist; the C++ Core Guidelines discuss expressing interfaces precisely and in the type system D4.
source: F12-02 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: a goal written so that a test or a measurement can say yes or no.
analogy: "the window is as wide as the table" instead of "a big window".
precise: a requirement stated as an observable condition with a method of observation (a test, an emulator scenario, a measurement procedure with its target); words like "fast" or "robust" are replaced by the observation that would show them. Curriculum rule 10's "exactly how the acceptance tests will observe success" asks for this D2.
source: F12-02 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: a decision that is not made yet, written down so nobody guesses.
analogy: the box "not decided yet: which way the back door opens".
precise: a numbered item in a design document that names an undecided point, who will decide it, by when or before which step, and what depends on it; the review's job includes deciding which open questions must be closed before code starts.
source: F12-02 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: a document that is changed whenever the thing it describes changes.
analogy: the blueprint on site gets the corrections, not a drawer copy.
precise: a design document kept in version control next to the code, with a status line (draft, in review, approved, implemented, superseded) and updated in the same change as the code it describes; the curriculum's definition of done includes "design note updated" D2; the F12 analogy row warns that software blueprints change more often D3.
source: F12-02 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: another way to meet the same goals.
analogy: another sketch of the same kitchen.
precise: a complete candidate design for the goals of a design document, described well enough that its costs and risks can be judged; the "Alternatives considered" section lists each with the reason it was not chosen, or the evidence that would choose it later. Course definition; D1 discusses alternatives in design documents D1.
source: F12-03 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: getting more of one good thing by accepting less of another.
analogy: a bigger window gives more light and leaves less wall for shelves.
precise: a relation between two or more criteria such that, among the available alternatives, improving one criterion requires giving up some of another; a design decision is an explicit choice of a point on that relation, justified by the goals.
source: F12-03 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: a table that scores each option on each thing you care about, with a weight for how much you care.
analogy: the team's points for each kitchen sketch.
precise: a table of criteria c with weights wc and scores sc,o for each option o, combined here as the weighted sum To = Σc wc sc,o; the weights and most scores are human judgements, and the table's value is to make them explicit and checkable, not to compute a truth. Listing 1 implements it.
source: F12-03 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: asking how much an input would have to change before the answer changes.
analogy: "how much more would we have to care about light before the other sketch wins?"
precise: for a weighted-sum matrix, for each criterion c and each challenger o, the weight change d at which Twinner − To + d (sc,winner − sc,o) = 0; the smallest |d| that keeps the weight non-negative shows how robust the decision is to that weight. Derived in Layer 3; Listing 1 computes it.
source: F12-03 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: an option that is no better than another option on anything, and worse on something.
analogy: a sketch with less light, less storage and a higher cost than another sketch.
precise: option a is dominated by option b if sc,a ≤ sc,b for every criterion c and sc,a < sc,b for at least one; whatever the non-negative weights, a cannot beat b, so a can be removed before any weighing.
source: F12-03 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: a choice that is cheap to undo later.
analogy: where the table stands (reversible) versus where the drain goes through the floor (not).
precise: a decision whose cost of reversal (code to change, data to migrate, callers to update, hardware state to recover) is small compared with the cost of deciding slowly; reversible decisions can be made quickly with a recorded revisit trigger, irreversible ones deserve more alternatives, more evidence and more reviewers (the "how much plan" table of F12-01).
source: F12-03 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: someone other than the author reads a change before it is accepted, and writes down what they find.
analogy: a second carpenter checks your joints (registered F12 mapping).
precise: a written examination of a proposed change (code, tests, documents) by one or more reviewers against the design document, the codebase's rules and their own experience, ending in a recorded decision (approve, or request changes) and a thread of comments the author answers; besides finding defects it spreads knowledge of the code, a purpose the registered analogy's "where it breaks" note names D3. D1 describes code review as practised in one large company D1.
source: F12-04 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: one proposed set of edits to the code, sent for review as a unit.
analogy: the new window frame, as one piece of work.
precise: a set of modifications to files, with a description of what and why, reviewed and accepted or rejected as a whole; in git, one or more commits on a branch; a good change does one thing, so its review has one question to answer.
source: F12-04 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: a printout of a change that shows removed lines with a minus, added lines with a plus, and a few unchanged lines around them.
analogy: a photo of the new frame with a little of the wall around it, but not the lintel.
precise: the output format of diff -u and of git diff: file headers (---, +++), then hunks headed @@ -l,s +l,s @@ giving the start line and length in the old and new file, with three lines of context by default; context shows only lines near a change, so code a change depends on may be invisible D4 R3.
source: F12-04 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: a word at the start of a review comment that says how much it matters.
analogy: "must fix before the glass goes in" versus "nicer finish if you have time".
precise: in this course, one of blocking (must be resolved before approval), suggestion (author decides), question (reviewer needs an answer to judge), nit (small style point, optional) and praise (specific good practice, so it is kept and copied); labels let the author sort the thread and stop small points from being read as demands.
source: F12-04 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: a comment that says "this must change before I can approve".
analogy: "the lintel may not hold; we check before the glass goes in".
precise: a review comment whose resolution is a condition of approval; in this course it must state the reason (the defect, risk or rule) and propose a change or ask the question that would settle it, and it is resolved only by a change or by the reviewer's recorded agreement (F12-05).
source: F12-04 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: a short list of questions a reviewer asks of every change.
analogy: the carpenter's habit of always looking at what a frame rests on.
precise: a written, short, project-specific list of questions applied to every change (boundaries, error paths, resource lifetimes, calling context and concurrency, units and interfaces, changed or deleted tests, untrusted inputs, sources for hardware facts), kept next to the code and extended after each incident whose cause a question would have caught.
source: F12-04 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: the person who wrote the change and asked for review.
analogy: the carpenter whose frame is being checked.
precise: the person responsible for a change until it is merged and afterwards: they describe it, answer every review comment, make and verify the fixes, and keep the design document and tests consistent with it. Course definition.
source: F12-05 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: the author's answer to one review comment.
analogy: the note Tomás pins under Kofi's note.
precise: in this course, exactly one of: fixed (with the commit that changes the code and, for a defect, the test that would have failed before it), answered (the reviewer asked a question; here is the answer, with evidence), wontfix (not changed, with the reason), or followup (agreed but out of scope; with the id of the issue that tracks it).
source: F12-05 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: a list of every comment and its answer, so nothing is forgotten.
analogy: the board where every pinned note and its answer stay until both carpenters agree.
precise: a record, one line per comment, of its label, location, response, reference (commit or issue) and the reviewer's agreement where needed; it checks bookkeeping (every comment answered, every "fixed" names a commit, every blocking comment closed by a change or by agreement), not whether a fix is correct. Listing 1 is one.
source: F12-05 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: a comment is closed only after someone checked that the fix fixes the thing the comment pointed at.
analogy: Kofi comes back and looks at the new lintel.
precise: the closing of a blocking comment after the reviewer (or the author, with evidence the reviewer accepts) has confirmed that the referenced change modifies the commented location or its cause and that a test reproducing the comment's scenario fails before the change and passes after it.
source: F12-05 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: a written task for later, made when a good comment does not belong in this change.
analogy: "repaint the hallway" goes on the list for next week.
precise: an entry in the project's issue tracker (or the design document's open questions) with an id, created during review for an agreed improvement outside the change's scope, referenced in the response so the comment can be closed without losing the point.
source: F12-05 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)

simple: asking a third person to decide when author and reviewer cannot agree.
analogy: asking the most experienced builder on site to look at the lintel with both of you.
precise: a step taken after both sides have stated their reasons and evidence in the thread: a named third person (another reviewer, the design document's approver, the teacher or mentor) decides, and the decision and its reason are recorded in the thread or the design document; escalation is about the decision, never about the person.
source: F12-05 (SE301 course definition; Systems Curriculum sections 5.4, 5.5 and 19.2 where cited in the chapter)
